items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1976-02-04
items.q: Duke was at the Cotton Club, you heard him on the radio

ctx.x: Do you, do you think that, that Jelly Roll Morton had the wide popularity among blacks that Louis Armstrong did when he was alive?

Never, never, never, never. Jelly, Jelly played in, clubs, and he made records that were popular, but to actually have, he moved around too fast. See, if he just stayed like, in Chicago, and worked in clubs, they stationary, like you make a reputation in the town, like Fletcher Henderson was in New York, Cab Calloway were in New York at the Cotton Club, Fletcher at the Roseland, you heard him on the radio, Duke was at the Cotton Club, you heard him on the radio, Earl Hines in, in the Grand Terrace in Chicago for…

do you think that, do you think that, that Louis Armstrong, was able to, keep his reputation, even though he traveled, or do you think that he built, his reputation in Chicago, and then when he traveled, it was already behind him?

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That’s what Duke Ellington did. He didn’t never work for nobody.

ctx.x: You just got to do your own thing. That’s what Duke Ellington did. He didn’t never work for nobody. [recording engineer:] This is Danny Barker, session two.

To put everything in perspective from the first session, we talked a lot about your early days, coming up in New Orleans in the [French] Quarter, about your parents and your family. We said that you had come from a quite extensive musical family. Do have any idea about how many musicians were in your family.

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: So I think Duke got some ideas from him. They said Duke's first band sounded something like what Jelly Roll had done already.

ctx.x: But he was practically around the first.
So I think Duke got some ideas from him. They said Duke's first band sounded something like what Jelly Roll had done already. I don't know if that's true.

Well, he certainly did... I don't have any recollection of anybody doing too much writing of the parts. He used to tell his men, "Just play them black notes. Just play what I put out on the paper for you."

items.title: Danny Barker Interview (Louis Armstrong memorial broadcast), 1971-07-09
items.q: It's like you take Duke Allen thing, you put him on the side.

ctx.x: The music is considered singers. Oh, I see. But then you become a stylist. I see what you're saying. See, with Larry coming on, you become an individual stylist. So people say, well, he always sings cute. See, like, whole Carmichael, people will buy his records. He's got a little thing like something about China, a nice little record. Well, you like it. Yeah, he was really reciting to his music, really. He's not a guy, but he's a stylist. I see what you're saying. You've seen Fats Waller come on, doing his humor.…
